content: Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) is a comprehensive, community-based approach designed to provide intensive support for individuals with severe and persistent mental illnesses. It is characterized by several key features: 1. Target Population: ACT focuses on individuals who require the highest level of support from the mental health care system. These are often individuals with complex needs who are at risk of homelessness or repeated hospitalizations. 2. Mission and Goals: The primary objectives of ACT are to prevent homelessness and unnecessary hospitalizations, while promoting independence, rehabilitation, and recovery for participants. 3. In Vivo Interventions: ACT emphasizes interventions conducted in real-world settings, such as participants' homes or community spaces, rather than in clinical offices. This eliminates the need to transfer learned behaviors from artificial treatment environments to everyday life. 4. Low Participant-to-Staff Ratio: ACT teams maintain a low participant-to-staff ratio, enabling the core team to directly provide nearly all necessary treatment, rehabilitation, and community support services. This is in contrast to traditional case management models, where much of the work is outsourced to other professionals. 5. Interdisciplinary Team: The ACT team typically includes a psychiatrist, nurses, social workers, substance abuse specialists, vocational rehabilitation counselors, and peer recovery specialists. These professionals collaborate to provide comprehensive assessments and service planning. 6. Responsibility for Well-Being: The ACT team assumes ultimate responsibility for participants' well-being across all areas of community functioning, including the practical aspects of daily life. 7. Crisis Prevention and Management: ACT teams work proactively to help participants avoid crises. If crises occur, the team provides immediate support at any time, day or night, without resorting to hospitalization. 8. Time-Unlimited Services: ACT teams commit to working with participants for as long as they demonstrate a need for this intensive level of professional support, regardless of measurable progress toward recovery. Early Development of ACT ACT was developed in the early 1970s during the deinstitutionalization movement, when large numbers of patients were discharged from state psychiatric hospitals into underdeveloped community service systems. The approach was pioneered by Leonard I. Stein, Arnold J. Marx, Deborah J. Test, William H. Allness, and their colleagues at the Mendota Mental Health Institute in Madison, Wisconsin. Initially known as the Training in Community Living (TCL) project or the Program of Assertive Community Treatment (PACT), it later became widely recognized as the Madison model. The original Madison project received the American Psychiatric Association's prestigious Gold Award in 1974. Initially designed to prevent hospitalization among a diverse group of prospective state hospital patients, the focus of ACT shifted in the late 1970s and 1980s to young adults with early-stage schizophrenia. ACT as an Evidence-Based Practice ACT has a long history of success with high-priority service recipients in various settings, as demonstrated by numerous rigorous outcome evaluation studies. It has been recognized as an evidence-based practice by organizations such as the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI), and the Commission on Accreditation of Rehabilitation Facilities (CARF). Despite its success, ACT has faced criticism. Some researchers, such as Jeffrey G. Geller and others, have argued that ACT is inherently coercive and that the research supporting it is scientifically flawed. However, proponents of ACT, including Stein and Test, have responded to these critiques, defending the model's validity and effectiveness. Dissemination of ACT Since the late 1970s, the ACT model has been widely replicated and adapted. The Harbinger program in Grand Rapids, Michigan, is considered the first replication, while a family-initiated adaptation in Minnesota also traces its origins to the Madison model. In 1978, the Bridge program at the Thresholds psychosocial rehabilitation center in Chicago became the first big-city adaptation of ACT, focusing on the most frequently hospitalized individuals with mental illness. In subsequent decades, Thresholds adapted the model to serve specific populations, including deaf individuals with mental illness, homeless individuals, those experiencing psychiatric crises, and individuals with mental illness who had been inappropriately jailed. In British Columbia, an experimental assertive outreach program based on the Thresholds model was established in 1988 and later expanded to additional sites. Outside North America, one of the first research-based adaptations was an assertive outreach program in Australia. Replications and adaptations of ACT can now be found throughout the English-speaking world. In Wisconsin, the original Madison model was adapted for rural environments. Major program concentrations exist in states such as Michigan, Indiana, Illinois, and others, as well as in countries like Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia. Research on ACT ACT is one of the most extensively studied intervention approaches in community mental health. The original Madison studies by Stein, Test, and their colleagues are considered classics in the field. Gary Bond, a prominent researcher, has been influential in developing fidelity measurement scales for ACT and other evidence-based practices. Bond and his colleagues have worked to consolidate and harmonize various service delivery styles and modifications of the ACT model to address specific challenges, such as co-occurring psychiatric and substance use disorders or competitive employment through supported employment programs. Funding and Expansion Initially, ACT programs were funded by grants from federal, state, or local mental health authorities. Over time, there has been a growing trend to fund these services through Medicaid and other publicly supported health insurance plans. Medicaid funding has facilitated the expansion of ACT into previously underserved areas, although challenges remain in demonstrating eligibility and securing supplemental funding for uncovered services. Future Directions Future program design and evaluation efforts should explore the integration of ACT with other established interventions, such as integrated dual disorders treatment, supported employment, family psychoeducation, and dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) for individuals with borderline personality disorder. The need for service integration remains a critical issue in community mental health, as it was when ACT was first developed.
